newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE-Move over Madonna -- it's the Japanese Evita.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Move over Madonna -- it's the Japanese Evita.

text.p: Akiko Kuno looks as much like Eva Peron as Madonna looks like Japan's Crown Princess Masako, but for Japanese the 47-year-old actress has been the face and voice of Evita for 15 years.

Jumping onto the bandwagon of "Evita-mania" and the hype around Alan Parker's musical movie starring Madonna, Japanese state television NHK is in Argentina paying its own homage to the glamorous champion of Argentina's poor and dispossessed, who died at the age of 33 in 1952.

The Argentine media, already bemused by the unlikely success of tango in Japan, are having great fun with the arrival of an oriental Evita. Madonna may have put the "Evita look" on the front pages of fashion magazines and her face on the Estee Lauder "Face of Evita" cosmetics line. But in Japan Kuno is so closely associated with the starring role in the Andrew Lloyd-Webber/Time Rice musical, a smash hit there when it it was translated into Japanese and staged in 1982, that her face was being used to promote an "Evita" perfume in Japan before anyone had thought of Madonna in the role.

"They must think my name is not Akiko but Eva," she told one interviewer here. Argentines are unlikely to make that mistake but they have given her a friendlier reception than they gave the iconoclastic U.S. pop star, whose casting was taken by some as an insult to the revered memory of Evita and who was greeted on arrival in Buenos Aires a year ago with graffiti proclaiming "Out With Madonna! Viva Evita!"
JAPANESE ACTRESS CHARMED ARGENTINE TV CREWS

Kuno's first visit to Plaza de Mayo, where the masses once flocked in their hundreds of thousands to cheer Juan and Eva Peron, went little noticed, although she charmed local television crews by singing a verse of "Don't Cry for Me Argentina" in Japanese.

Behind her was the balcony of the Pink House palace where Evita used her blend of sex appeal, bullying and fragility to rally her beloved "descamisados" (shirtless ones) to Peron, the populist general who was the elected president of Argentina from 1946-55 and again in 1973-74.
The balcony has had a busy year.

First it was Madonna singing "Don't Cry for Me..." to a mistrusting Argentina and rave reviews in the United States, where the movie grossed nearly $9 million in its first weekend and shot to No. 2 at the box-office. Then there was the low-budget loyalist Argentine response, with ethereal local actress Esther Goris going on a dangerous diet to portray Evita in her painful final months of life.

Now NHK wants permission from current Peronist President Carlos Menem to use the balcony for its 90-minute biography, mixing drama and music with interviews and archive shots that Kuno promises will "try to show the real Eva, the one in the musical and the one in the hearts of all Argentines."

But the actress herself is apparently still of two minds about Eva Peron, the poor girl from the province who caught General Peron's eye when she was a small-time radio star trying to make it in the movies and was still a brunette.

In Argentina, Evita is still revered by some as a saint for her apparent devotion to the poor, to whom she dished out clothes, cash and sewing machines. Others saw her as a vulgar, ruthless demogogue who slept her way to power and squandered Argentina's wealth to buy the votes of the working class.

"I want to see how Evita is remembered in Argentina after so many years -- if she is hated or not, if she is a demon or an angel. That's what I've come to find out," said Kuno, who will make pilgrimages for the film to Evita's tomb in Buenos Aires' elegant Recoleta cemetery and to her humble birthplace in Los Toldos, a small town in Buenos Aires Province.

In Kuno's homeland, Evita's memory is definitely angelic. The glamorous blonde "Champion of the Poor" is gratefully remembered there for the food and clothes sent by her charity, the Eva Peron Foundation, to hungry post-war Japan in 1948.

Fading black-and-white photographs from the time show small Japanese children holding a picture of Evita and toys sent by her and the South American benefactress' face beams from the cover of a Japanese newspaper of 1949.

"Evita has a special attraction for the Japanese. We heard of her after the war, when she sent food for the poor," Kuno said. "Although I'm of another generation, I grew up admiring her. Evita is a myth in Japan just like she is in Argentina."
